reasoning: Extensive scientific research and double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have failed to establish a causal relationship between monosodium glutamate (MSG) consumed in normal dietary amounts and symptoms such as headaches, numbness, or flushing (historically labeled "Chinese restaurant syndrome"). Major food safety and public health authorities—including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA)—classify MSG as "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS). The glutamate in MSG is chemically indistinguishable from glutamate naturally found in foods like tomatoes, aged cheeses, and mushrooms. The myth originated largely from an anecdotal 1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine and subsequent poorly controlled early studies influenced by xenophobic biases.
title: MSG causes headaches — 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'
